Security triad: keep data private, accurate, and available when needed.
Legacy symmetric encryption that is now considered insecure.
Legacy stream cipher that should not be used for modern secure systems.
Modern symmetric encryption. AES-256 uses a 256-bit key for stronger protection.
Public-key cryptosystem used for encryption and digital signatures.
Temporary key exchange method that supports perfect forward secrecy.
Public-key cryptography that gives strong security with smaller keys than RSA.
Elliptic-curve temporary key exchange used for forward secrecy.
Elliptic-curve method for creating and verifying digital signatures.
Protects past session keys even if a server private key is later exposed.
Hash family that creates fixed-length digests for integrity checks.
Uses a hash and secret key to verify message integrity and authenticity.
Shared secret configured before two systems authenticate.
People, policies, certificates, and systems used to manage certificate-based trust.
Trusted organization or service that issues and signs digital certificates.
PKI role that verifies identity before certificate issuance.
Request sent to a CA when asking for a signed certificate.
Published list of certificates that should no longer be trusted.
Real-time method for checking whether a certificate has been revoked.
Protocol that helps devices request and receive certificates automatically.
Common text format for certificates and keys.
Standards for handling public-key cryptography, keys, and certificates.
Hardware chip used to store keys and support device integrity checks.
Dedicated hardware for protecting cryptographic keys and performing sensitive crypto operations.
IPsec protocol that provides integrity and source authentication but not encryption.
Authentication framework commonly used with wireless and network access.
Legacy Cisco wireless authentication method vulnerable to password attacks.
Legacy protocol that sends passwords in cleartext and should be avoided.

cards.definition: Challenge used to reduce automated bot activity.
Smart-card standard used for physical and logical access in U.S. federal environments.
Access model where the data owner decides who can access an object.
Access model where labels and central policy decide access, not the object owner.
Access is assigned through job roles such as analyst, admin, or manager.
Access is decided by rules such as location, device state, or time of day.
Ordered permission list that allows or denies access to a file, folder, device, or network rule.
Access is allowed only during approved time windows.
Framework for proving identity, deciding permitted actions, and recording activity.
Service that stores identity data and authenticates users for applications.
Centralized AAA protocol often used for VPN, Wi-Fi, and network access.

cards.full_form: Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus
keywords: Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus
cards.definition: AAA protocol commonly used for network-device administration.
Lets users sign in once and access multiple trusted applications.
Standard used to exchange login and authorization data between identity systems.
Delegated authorization that lets an app access limited resources without seeing the password.
Identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 used for login and user identity claims.
Uses two or more factor types, such as password plus authenticator app.
Standard format for describing threat intelligence.

cards.full_form: Trusted Automated eXchange of Indicator Information
keywords: TAXII (Trusted Automated eXchange of Indicator Information)
Trusted Automated eXchange of Indicator Information
cards.definition: Protocol used to exchange STIX threat intelligence.
Standard used to automate vulnerability and configuration checking.
Uses a believable invented story to manipulate a victim.
cards.example: A caller claims to run a routine security audit and asks for login details.

cards.definition: Pretends to be a trusted person, authority, or brand.
cards.example: An attacker wearing a vendor polo and holding a clipboard requests server-room access.

cards.definition: Compromises a site frequently visited by the intended target group.
cards.example: A defense-industry forum is infected because employees from one contractor visit it daily.

cards.definition: Broad message-based attempt to trick users into revealing information or taking unsafe action.
cards.example: Many users receive a fake password-reset email linking to a credential-harvesting page.

cards.definition: Targeted phishing aimed at a specific person or organization.
cards.example: A finance clerk receives a dean-branded email requesting an urgent payment update.

cards.definition: Phishing aimed at executives or other high-profile targets.
cards.example: A CEO receives a fake legal subpoena email that pressures them to log into a portal.

cards.definition: Social engineering performed through phone calls.
cards.example: A caller claims to be IT support and asks an employee to verify their password.

cards.definition: Social engineering performed through text messages.
cards.example: A package-delivery text says to click a link and enter card details.

cards.definition: Impersonates business leaders or partners to trick employees into payments or data release.
cards.example: A spoofed CFO email asks accounting to urgently wire $50,000 to a vendor.

cards.definition: Registers lookalike or mistyped domain names to catch user mistakes.
cards.example: A fake paypa1.com login page captures credentials from users who mistype the domain.

cards.definition: Follows an authorized person into a restricted area without using credentials.
cards.example: An attacker carrying coffee walks behind an employee through a badge-controlled door.

cards.definition: Searches discarded materials for sensitive information.
cards.example: A competitor finds unshredded pricing documents in a company's recycling bin.

cards.definition: Observes a screen, keypad, or paper to steal sensitive information.
cards.example: Someone watches a debit-card PIN being entered from close behind in a queue.

cards.definition: Uses physical tampering or environmental disruption to damage or weaken systems.
cards.example: Power lines to a data center are cut, forcing systems into unsafe recovery conditions.

cards.definition: Compromises a trusted vendor, update path, or service provider to reach victims.
cards.example: An HVAC vendor is breached and its credentials are used to access a retail client.

cards.definition: Untrusted input is interpreted as a command or query by a vulnerable system.
cards.example: A user types special characters into a form and the server treats them as executable instructions.

cards.definition: Attack that inserts SQL commands into application input to access or change data.
cards.example: Typing ' OR '1'='1 into a login field bypasses authentication on a vulnerable app.

cards.definition: Application input is used to run unauthorized operating-system commands.
cards.example: A ping tool accepts 127.0.0.1; cat /etc/passwd and returns internal account data.

cards.definition: Path manipulation accesses files outside the intended directory.
cards.example: Changing a file viewer URL to ../../../../etc/passwd reveals restricted system files.

cards.definition: Web attack that runs malicious script in another user's browser.
cards.example: A forum comment injects script that steals session cookies from people who view the post.

cards.definition: Attack that tricks a signed-in user into submitting an unwanted action.
cards.example: A hidden image request causes a logged-in banking user to submit a transfer unknowingly.

cards.definition: Tricks a backend server into making unauthorized internal or external requests.
cards.example: A URL box is pointed at cloud metadata, causing the server to expose internal credentials.

cards.definition: Targets weak API authentication, authorization, validation, or rate limiting.
cards.example: Changing /user/1001/profile to /user/1002/profile reveals another user's data.

cards.definition: Too much data is written into memory, causing corruption or possible code execution.
cards.example: A field built for 20 characters receives 2,000 characters and overwrites nearby memory.

cards.definition: Malicious code is inserted into a running process to hide or execute activity.
cards.example: Malware injects a DLL into notepad.exe to run while avoiding simple file scans.

cards.definition: Exploits timing gaps between a security check and the later action.
cards.example: A withdraw button is triggered twice before the account balance update completes.

cards.definition: A user or process gains higher permissions than intended.
cards.example: A guest web account exploits a kernel flaw to gain root administrator access.

cards.definition: Tries many possible passwords or keys until one works.
cards.example: An automated tool tries 0001, 0002, 0003, and so on against a four-digit PIN.

cards.definition: Uses a wordlist of common passwords and variations to guess credentials.
cards.example: A login script tries 50,000 common words and substitutions such as P@ssword1.

cards.definition: Tests a few common passwords across many accounts to avoid lockouts.
cards.example: Winter2026! is tried against 5,000 email accounts to find weak users.

cards.definition: Reuses stolen credentials or session tokens to gain access.
cards.example: A stolen session cookie is added to another browser to access someone else's account.

cards.definition: Uses precomputed hash lookups to recover plaintext passwords from hashes.
cards.example: A known MD5 hash is looked up and instantly revealed as the password 'password'.

cards.definition: Forces a system to use weaker legacy security instead of stronger modern protection.
cards.example: A browser connection is manipulated to fall back from modern TLS to legacy SSL.

cards.definition: Finds two different inputs that produce the same hash value.
cards.example: Two contract files are crafted to share the same SHA-1 hash, hiding a malicious version.

cards.definition: Uses probability to find hash collisions faster than simple guessing.
cards.example: Random message variants are generated until two produce matching hashes by chance.

cards.definition: Attack that makes a service unavailable to legitimate users.
cards.example: A single attacker overwhelms a public web server until normal users cannot reach it.

cards.definition: Availability attack using many systems to overwhelm a target.
cards.example: Thousands of infected smart cameras send fake traffic to an online store and take it offline.

cards.definition: Spoofs the victim address so third-party systems send response traffic to the victim.
cards.example: An attacker spoofs a bank IP in requests to many routers, causing replies to flood the bank.

cards.definition: Uses protocols with larger replies than requests to multiply traffic sent to a victim.
cards.example: A tiny NTP query causes a vulnerable server to send a much larger reply to the victim.

cards.definition: Attacker secretly intercepts or changes communication between two parties.
cards.example: A coffee-shop Wi-Fi attacker reads unencrypted login traffic between a laptop and website.

cards.definition: Manipulates DNS so users are redirected, misled, or unable to resolve names.
cards.example: Users typing a bank domain are redirected to a fake site after poisoned DNS data is cached.

cards.definition: Sends false IP-to-MAC mappings so local traffic flows through the attacker.
cards.example: A laptop announces 'I am the gateway' so nearby computers send traffic through it.

cards.definition: Manipulates switch tagging to reach traffic on a different VLAN.
cards.example: Double-tagged 802.1Q frames move traffic from a guest network toward the HR VLAN.

cards.definition: Unauthorized wireless access point connected to a trusted network.
cards.example: An employee plugs a home router into an office network jack, bypassing approved wireless controls.

cards.definition: Malicious Wi-Fi access point that imitates a trusted network name.
cards.example: A fake Airport_Free_WiFi network records credentials from travelers who join it.

cards.definition: Radio interference used to disrupt wireless communication.
cards.example: A thief uses an RF transmitter to block a home security camera signal during a break-in.

cards.definition: Forged wireless management frames force clients to disconnect from Wi-Fi.
cards.example: Fake deauth frames kick a laptop off corporate Wi-Fi so it reconnects to an evil twin.

cards.definition: Copies contactless identifiers to bypass physical access controls.
cards.example: A hidden scanner copies an employee badge on the subway for later building access.

cards.definition: Malware that encrypts or blocks access to data until payment is demanded.
cards.example: Office spreadsheets become encrypted and a message demands Bitcoin for the unlock key.

cards.definition: Malware disguised as legitimate or useful software.
cards.example: A free PDF converter also installs a hidden backdoor on the device.

cards.definition: Self-replicating malware that spreads automatically across networks.
cards.example: Malware scans for open SMB ports and copies itself to other machines without user action.

cards.definition: Malicious code that attaches to legitimate files and spreads when they run.
cards.example: An infected installer.exe on a USB drive infects the next computer that runs it.

cards.definition: Malware that secretly monitors user activity or collects personal information.
cards.example: A phone app quietly uploads GPS location and browsing history to an advertising group.

cards.definition: Software or hardware that records keystrokes such as passwords or PINs.
cards.example: A hidden USB device between a keyboard and computer records every typed password.

cards.definition: Stealth malware that hides itself while maintaining privileged system control.
cards.example: Kernel-level malware changes OS APIs so Task Manager cannot show the malicious process.

cards.definition: Malicious code that activates only when a condition, event, or date occurs.
cards.example: A script deletes a database when a former developer's employee ID is disabled.

cards.definition: Trojan malware that gives an attacker remote control of the victim system.
cards.example: A fake utility installs a backdoor that lets the attacker control the computer remotely.

cards.definition: Unwanted preinstalled software that can increase risk and attack surface.
cards.example: A new laptop includes unnecessary trial apps, including one with an unpatched vulnerability.

cards.definition: Software that may be unwanted or risky even if not always classed as malware.
cards.example: A browser toolbar tracks searches and injects ads after being bundled with free software.

cards.definition: Trusted software updates are compromised to distribute malware.
cards.example: A vendor update package is trojanized and pushes malware to many customers.

cards.definition: Breaks out of a guest virtual machine to reach the host or other guests.
cards.example: A cloud VM exploit gives access to the physical host running other customers' workloads.

cards.definition: Installs apps from untrusted sources outside approved app stores.
cards.example: A downloaded APK from a file-sharing forum installs adware with the promised app.

cards.definition: Bypasses mobile operating-system restrictions and weakens built-in protections.
cards.example: An exploit removes iOS sandbox restrictions so root-level apps can be installed.

cards.definition: Targets low-level device code such as BIOS or UEFI for persistent control.
cards.example: Modified motherboard firmware reinstalls malware after every reboot, even after disk formatting.

cards.definition: Software that detects, blocks, or removes malware.
Filters web application traffic to help block attacks such as SQL injection and XSS.
Web security tool that filters unsafe web traffic and user browsing.
Controls that help stop sensitive data from leaving approved locations.
Detects unauthorized or unexpected changes to important files.
Wireless tools that detect or block rogue access points and wireless attacks.

cards.full_form: Domain-Based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance
keywords: Domain-Based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance
cards.definition: Email protection policy that uses SPF and DKIM results to reduce spoofing.
Email signature method that helps prove a message was authorized by a domain.
Network that connects systems in a limited area such as an office or home.
Logical network segment used to separate traffic on switches.
Screened subnet that exposes public-facing services while keeping the internal network separated.
Another term for a DMZ: a controlled subnet between the internet and internal network.
Private internal network used by an organization's employees.
Controlled private network that allows limited access for trusted external partners or customers.
Hardened system used to administer assets in a separate or protected security zone.
Physical isolation where a system or network is disconnected from other networks, including the internet.
Traffic moving laterally between systems inside a data center or internal network.
Traffic entering or leaving a network boundary, such as internet-to-server communication.
Dividing networks or cloud workloads into small isolated zones to limit lateral movement.
Boundary-focused design that trusts internal traffic more than external traffic; common in older network models.
Layered security strategy where multiple controls protect assets if one control fails.
Separates network control from hardware forwarding to enable programmable networks.
Uses software policies to route WAN traffic across available links.
Network routing method that forwards traffic using labels.
Management layer that handles administration, policies, authentication decisions, and routing control.
Operational layer that forwards user traffic according to decisions made by the control plane.
Cloud-delivered model combining network access and security controls.
Security model based on never trust, always verify with continuous checks for users, devices, and sessions.
Encrypted tunnel that protects traffic across an untrusted network.
Core protocol suite used by the Internet and most modern networks.
Protocol used for network messages such as ping and error reporting.
Maps an IP address to a MAC address on a local network.
Automatically assigns IP addresses and network settings to devices.
Translates domain names into IP addresses.

cards.full_form: Network Address Translation / Port Address Translation
keywords: Network Address Translation / Port Address Translation
cards.definition: Maps private internal addresses to public addresses; PAT also tracks ports.
Protocol used to query and update directory services.
Microsoft protocol for remote graphical access to another computer.
Encrypted remote administration protocol, commonly used for command-line access.
Synchronizes clocks across systems and network devices.
Decentralized model where systems communicate directly with each other.
Unique hardware address assigned to a network interface.

cards.full_form: Secure Sockets Layer / Transport Layer Security
keywords: Secure Sockets Layer / Transport Layer Security
cards.definition: Legacy and modern protocols for encrypted network communication; TLS replaced SSL.
Protocol suite that authenticates and encrypts IP traffic, often for VPNs.

cards.full_form: File Transfer Protocol Secure / SSH File Transfer Protocol
keywords: File Transfer Protocol Secure / SSH File Transfer Protocol
cards.definition: Secure file-transfer options; FTPS uses TLS and SFTP uses SSH.
Protocol for collecting and managing network device information.

cards.full_form: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol / Secure SMTP
keywords: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol / Secure SMTP
cards.definition: Email-sending protocol and its TLS-protected form.
Adds encryption and integrity protection to real-time voice or video traffic.
Wireless device that lets Wi-Fi clients connect to a wired network.

cards.full_form: Wi-Fi Protected Access / Wired Equivalent Privacy
keywords: Wi-Fi Protected Access / Wired Equivalent Privacy
cards.definition: Wireless security standards; WEP is obsolete and insecure, while WPA versions are newer.

cards.full_form: Infrastructure / Platform / Software as a Service
keywords: Infrastructure / Platform / Software as a Service
cards.definition: Cloud service models with different responsibility split between customer and provider.
Serverless cloud model where event-driven functions run without the customer managing servers.
Security service between cloud users and cloud apps that enforces policy.
Cloud infrastructure owned by a third-party provider and accessed over the internet.
Cloud infrastructure used by one organization, hosted on-premises or by a provider.
Environment that connects private cloud or on-premises resources with public cloud services.
Cloud environment shared by organizations with common security, compliance, or mission requirements.
Isolated virtual network inside a cloud provider environment.
Cloud security split where the provider secures the cloud infrastructure and the customer secures data, identity, and configurations.
Software-based computer running inside another physical or virtual system.
Legacy firmware that starts hardware before the operating system loads.
Software that manages hardware, apps, users, files, and system resources.
Chip that combines many computer components into one integrated circuit.
Processor often used for graphics, high-speed computation, machine learning, or password cracking.
Storage device types; HDD is mechanical and SSD uses flash memory.
Network-connected physical devices such as sensors, cameras, and smart devices.
Systems used to monitor or control physical industrial processes.
Industrial control system used to monitor and control physical processes.

cards.full_form: Bring Your Own Device / Corporate-Owned Personally Enabled / Choose Your Own Device
keywords: Bring Your Own Device / Corporate-Owned Personally Enabled / Choose Your Own Device
cards.definition: Mobile-device ownership models with different security and privacy tradeoffs.
Tooling used to manage and enforce policy on mobile devices.
Central tool for managing desktops, laptops, mobile devices, and other endpoints.
Rules that let applications communicate with each other.
Tools and libraries used to build software for a platform.

cards.full_form: Software Development Life Cycle / Software Development Life-Cycle Methodology
keywords: Software Development Life Cycle / Software Development Life-Cycle Methodology
cards.definition: Structured process for planning, building, testing, and maintaining software securely.
Managing infrastructure through code files instead of manual configuration.
Computer systems that perform tasks that normally require human intelligence, such as pattern recognition.
AI approach where systems improve from data patterns instead of explicit step-by-step rules.
Shared Windows code library used by multiple programs.
Windows mechanism for handling program and system exceptions.
Memory protection that helps stop code from running in non-executable memory areas.
Linux security module that enforces stronger access-control policies.

cards.full_form: Power Distribution Unit / Uninterruptible Power Supply
keywords: Power Distribution Unit / Uninterruptible Power Supply
cards.definition: Power distribution and backup power equipment used for availability.
Stored data that is not actively moving, such as files, databases, drives, or backups.
Data moving across a network, cable, wireless link, or other communication path.
Data currently being processed in memory, CPU registers, or an active application.
Replacing sensitive data with a token that has no useful value outside the token vault.
Hiding or altering sensitive characters so data can be used without exposing full details.
Irreversibly removing identifying links so individuals cannot be re-identified.
Replacing identifiers with pseudonyms while keeping a separate mapping that can re-identify the person if authorized.
Architecture goal that keeps services operating through redundancy and fast failover.
Ability of a system to keep operating when one or more components fail.
Distributing traffic across multiple systems to improve availability and performance.
Spreading systems across regions so one local disaster does not take down the whole service.
Storage design that combines disks for performance, redundancy, or both depending on RAID level.
Disk striping for performance only; it does not provide redundancy.
Disk mirroring where data is duplicated across drives for redundancy.
Disk striping with parity that requires at least three drives and can tolerate one drive failure.
Disk striping with dual parity that can tolerate two simultaneous drive failures.
Fully operational recovery facility with hardware, software, and data ready for quick failover.
Partially prepared recovery facility that has infrastructure but needs current data restored.
Basic recovery facility with utilities but little or no installed computing equipment.
Approved minimum security configuration applied consistently to systems, applications, and network devices.
Reducing attack surface by disabling unneeded services, closing unused ports, removing unnecessary software, and changing defaults.
Execution control where allow lists permit approved software and block lists deny prohibited software.
Running suspicious or untrusted software in a restricted environment so it cannot easily affect the host.
Tools that detect suspicious activity on a host or across network traffic.
Tools that can block suspicious activity on a host or network.
Endpoint tool that monitors activity and supports investigation and containment.

cards.full_form: Encrypting File System / Full Disk Encryption
keywords: Encrypting File System / Full Disk Encryption
cards.definition: File-level and whole-disk encryption methods for protecting stored data.
Storage drive that automatically encrypts data on the device.
File-level permission list used to control access to files and folders.
Microsoft Active Directory feature used to centrally enforce configuration, password, and security settings.
Alternative control used when the primary control, such as immediate patching, cannot be applied.
Granting only the minimum access needed for a user, process, or system to do its job.
Controls and tools used to secure, monitor, and audit administrator or root-level access.
Temporary privileged access granted only when needed and removed after the task or time window ends.
Creating, changing, and removing accounts and permissions across a user lifecycle.
Standard used by systems and network devices to send event messages to a central logging server.
Network telemetry that summarizes IP traffic flows using metadata rather than full packet contents.
Standard for exporting IP flow metadata such as source, destination, ports, and packet counts.
Collecting logs from many sources into one central place for searching, alerting, and investigation.
Using controls such as hashing to prove logs were not altered, deleted, or tampered with.
Central team or function that monitors, detects, and responds to security events.
Platform that collects and correlates logs for alerting and investigation.
Automates repeatable response workflows using playbooks.
Correlates detection and response data across endpoints, network, cloud, and other sources.
Behavior-based analytics that flags unusual user or device activity compared with a normal baseline.
External provider that supplies security monitoring or operations services.
Public naming system that gives known vulnerabilities standardized identifiers.
Standard scoring method used to rate vulnerability severity, commonly from 0.0 to 10.0.
Automated process for finding and reporting known weaknesses in systems, devices, or applications.
Alert or scan result that reports a problem even though the problem is not actually present.
Failure to detect a real vulnerability or malicious activity that is actually present.
Process of testing and applying software updates that fix bugs or security weaknesses.
Written process for responding to a cyber incident.

cards.full_form: Computer Incident Response Team / Computer Emergency Response Team
keywords: Computer Incident Response Team / Computer Emergency Response Team
cards.definition: Team responsible for handling cybersecurity incidents.

cards.full_form: Chief Information Officer / Chief Security Officer
keywords: Chief Information Officer / Chief Security Officer
cards.definition: Senior leaders responsible for IT direction and security risk.
Document that tracks a problem, root cause, and corrective action.
Documented step-by-step procedure analysts follow during repeatable incident response tasks.

cards.full_form: Preparation, Identification, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, and Lessons Learned
keywords: PICERL (Preparation, Identification, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, Lessons Learned)
Preparation, Identification, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, and Lessons Learned
cards.definition: Common incident response lifecycle used to structure breach handling from readiness through review.
Incident response phase focused on isolating affected systems to stop spread or further damage.
Incident response phase where malware, attacker access, and related artifacts are removed.
Forensic collection priority that gathers the most temporary evidence, such as RAM, before less volatile storage.
Chronological record of who collected, handled, transferred, and protected evidence.
Directive to preserve relevant records when litigation or investigation is expected.
Capture of system RAM for analysis of running processes, connections, credentials, and injected code.
Plan for restoring IT systems after a major outage or disaster.
Average time needed to repair a failure or restore service.
Rules, structures, and leadership processes that align security work with business goals, laws, and risk limits.
Leadership group that reviews security strategy, risk, major policies, and priorities across the organization.
Formal program for managing security policies, risk treatment, controls, and continuous improvement.
Standards organization associated with security frameworks such as ISO/IEC 27001.

cards.full_form: National Institute of Standards and Technology
keywords: National Institute of Standards and Technology
cards.definition: U.S. organization that publishes widely used cybersecurity guidance.
Structured guidance for managing security risk, commonly associated with the NIST CSF functions.
Organization known for CIS Benchmarks, which give secure configuration guidance for systems and cloud services.
EU privacy law that protects personal data of people in the EU and EEA.

cards.full_form: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
keywords: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
cards.definition: U.S. law that sets privacy and security requirements for protected health information.

cards.full_form: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard
keywords: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard
cards.definition: Security standard for organizations that store, process, or transmit payment-card data.
Information that can identify, contact, or locate a person.
Health information that can identify a person.
Clear assignment of responsibility for classifying, protecting, using, and handling data correctly.
Senior business role responsible for a dataset's classification, protection requirements, and approved use.
Privacy role that decides why and how personal data is processed.
Third party that processes personal data on behalf of a data controller.
Technical role that maintains data and implements controls such as storage, backups, access, and retention.
Contract term that gives an organization permission to inspect or audit a vendor's controls and processes.
Risk analysis that uses numbers and money values, such as AV, EF, SLE, ARO, and ALE.
Risk analysis that uses descriptive ratings such as high, medium, low, or a numbered risk matrix.
Central list of risks, owners, impact, likelihood, status, and selected treatment plans.
Broad amount of risk an organization is willing to accept while pursuing its goals.
Acceptable variation from the organization's risk appetite for a specific situation or system.
Percentage of an asset's value expected to be lost from one risk event.
Expected loss from one occurrence of a risk.
How often a risk is expected to happen in one year.
Expected yearly loss from a risk. Formula: SLE × ARO.
Decision to acknowledge a risk and continue without adding more controls.
Decision to stop or change an activity so the risk is removed.
Use of controls to lower the likelihood or impact of a risk.
Shifting financial impact to another party, such as insurance or a contract provider.
Process that identifies critical functions and the business impact of downtime.
Plan for keeping critical business functions running during disruption.
Plan for maintaining essential operations during emergencies.
Target time for restoring a process or service after disruption.
Maximum acceptable data loss measured in time.
Average time between failures for a repairable system.
Expected operating time before a non-repairable component fails.
Measure used to compare benefit against cost.
Unique identifier used to name objects in systems such as PKI, SNMP, and directories.
Agreement defining service expectations such as uptime or response time.
Contract that sets broad terms for future work between parties.
Document describing project work, deliverables, and timelines.
Legal agreement that requires parties to protect confidential information.
Agreement defining responsibilities and security expectations between business partners.

cards.full_form: Memorandum of Agreement / Memorandum of Understanding
keywords: Memorandum of Agreement / Memorandum of Understanding
cards.definition: Documents that define cooperation and shared responsibilities between organizations.
Organization that provides Internet connectivity.
Review of a supplier's security, compliance, and operational risk before or during a business relationship.
Risk introduced through external software, hardware, vendors, service providers, or business partners.
Security training tailored to a person's job duties, such as developers, finance staff, or executives.
Controlled phishing tests used to measure reporting behavior and provide quick retraining.
Use of points, challenges, or competition to make security training more engaging.
Interactive security challenge format used for training, practice, and awareness activities.
